modules.name: 6-Axis IMU (ICM-40608 or LSM6DSOX)
modules.description: 6-axis inertial measurement unit with 3-axis accelerometer (±2g), 3-axis gyroscope (±250°/s), and on-die temperature. The driver auto-detects which chip is attached at boot (ICM-40608 at 0x68 or LSM6DSOX at 0x6A) — generated user code is identical either way. Background RTOS task polls at 100Hz, readings are instant.
modules.use_for: Feels tilting, shaking and turning, so your project can react to how it is moved.
modules.how_it_works:
6-AXIS IMU (ORIENTATION SENSOR):
- Background RTOS task polls the chip at 100Hz. All getters return cached
  values instantly — never blocking, safe to call every loop iteration.
- PREFER DERIVED HELPERS over raw axes. Users almost always want "tilt",
  "shake", or "which way is up" — not three raw float streams. Reach for
  raw axes only when the user explicitly asks for gyro/accel values, a
  custom fusion algorithm, or scientific logging.

DERIVED API (use these first):
- getPitch()  -> degrees, -90..+90 (nose up positive). Accel-based, so it's
                 accurate when the board is roughly still but noisy under
                 acceleration. Good for tilt-to-control UIs.
- getRoll()   -> degrees, -180..+180 (left/right). Same caveat as pitch.
- getTiltAngle() -> degrees from upright. 0 = flat face-up, 90 = on its
                    side, 180 = flat face-down. Best single value for
                    "is the board tilted" questions.
- getOrientation() -> ICM40608::Orientation enum (ORI_FACE_UP, ORI_FACE_DOWN,
                      ORI_EDGE_RIGHT, ORI_EDGE_LEFT, ORI_EDGE_FRONT,
                      ORI_EDGE_BACK, ORI_UNKNOWN). Switches when one axis
                      clearly dominates (>0.7g) — has natural hysteresis
                      between faces.
- getOrientationName() -> const char* "face_up" / "face_down" / "edge_*" /
                          "unknown". Convenient for printing/events.
- wasShaken() -> true ONCE per shake/tap (>1.8g spike). Edge-triggered:
                 reading it clears the flag. Poll it once per loop:
                   if (imu.wasShaken()) { trigger_thing(); }
                 For a "real shake gesture" (vs. a single tap), require
                 2-3 wasShaken() events within ~500ms before reacting.
- setShakeThreshold(g) -> tune sensitivity. Default 1.8g. Drop to ~1.4 for
                          light taps, raise to ~2.5 for vigorous shakes.

RAW API (only when needed):
- readAccelX/Y/Z()  -> float g, ±2g full-scale.
- readGyroX/Y/Z()   -> float deg/s, ±250°/s full-scale.
- At rest with the module flat face-up, readAccelZ() ≈ +1.0 and X/Y ≈ 0.
- Gyro has small zero-offset bias. If you read raw gyro, call
  calibrateGyro() ONCE in setup() with the board stationary — it averages
  100 samples and subtracts the bias from every subsequent read.

PATTERNS:
- Tilt → output mapping (LEDs, screens, motors): scale pitch/roll directly.
  Example: int hue = (int)((getRoll() + 180.0f) * 255.0f / 360.0f);
- Detect "face down" gesture: if (imu.getOrientationName() == "face_down").
  To avoid flapping, require it to stay there for ~200ms (track last
  orientation + a millis() timestamp).
- Shake-to-trigger: just `if (imu.wasShaken()) { ... }`. Don't try to roll
  your own threshold from raw accel — the driver already does it.
- "Is the board moving?" — use total gyro magnitude:
    float w = sqrtf(gx*gx + gy*gy + gz*gz);  // deg/s
    bool moving = w > 30.0f;

AXES & ORIENTATION:
- The IMU's axes are the chip's axes, in the module's PCB frame: +Y points
  outward from the connector toward the module's free end, +X is one
  quarter-turn clockwise of +Y seen from above, +Z up out of the face.
  setMountRotation(deg) turns X-Y into the board frame (+X right edge, +Y
  top edge); the server's setup_order gives the degrees for the port
  (p2p/phases/firmware.py MOUNT_ROTATION_BY_EDGE). pitch/roll/orientation
  assume the board lies flat; mounted vertically, their meaning rotates
  with it. Tell the user this if their layout depends on orientation.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: Three live linear gauges (X / Y / Z) for accelerometer or gyro values that update from incoming sensor events. Add a small 3D orientation indicator (rotating cube or plane) that reflects the live pose, and a 60-second sparkline per axis below.

modules.name: AHT20 Temperature & Humidity Sensor
modules.description: Integrated temperature (-40 to +125°C) and humidity (0-100%RH) sensor. Background RTOS task measures every 2s — readings are instant.
modules.use_for: Measures how warm and how damp the air around your project is.
modules.how_it_works:
AHT20 TEMPERATURE & HUMIDITY SENSOR:
- readTemperature() returns float in Celsius. readHumidity() returns float 0-100 %RH.
- Sensor runs in a background FreeRTOS task (reads every 2s automatically).
- Calling readTemperature()/readHumidity() returns the latest cached value — it's instant, not blocking.
- Don't read faster than every 500ms — the sensor update rate is fixed at ~2s.
- Values are valid after begin() completes. First read may return 0 briefly.

modules.how_it_works:
SCD40 AIR QUALITY SENSOR (CO2 + temp + humidity):
- readCO2() returns uint16_t ppm. readTemperature() returns float Celsius. readHumidity() returns float 0-100 %RH.
- Sensor runs in a background FreeRTOS task. New measurements arrive every ~5s (sensor cadence).
- All getters return the latest cached value — instant, never blocking.
- readCO2() returns 0 until the first measurement lands (~5s after boot). Guard initial UI with isReady() if needed.
- Indoor CO2 reference: <800 ppm fresh, 800-1200 ppm acceptable, >1500 ppm poor (sleepy/distracted), >2000 ppm uncomfortable.
- Don't poll faster than every 500ms — the underlying sensor only updates every 5s.

modules.name: VL53L5CX 8x8 Distance Sensor
modules.description: 8x8 multi-zone Time-of-Flight distance sensor (up to 4m). Provides 64 distance measurements in a grid. Background RTOS task ranges at 15Hz — readings are instant. SCL on Line A, SDA on Line B.
modules.use_for: Sees how far away things are, so your project can notice people or objects coming close.
modules.how_it_works:
VL53L5CX DISTANCE SENSOR — RESPONSIVE PRESENCE PATTERN:
- Readings are instant (background task at 15Hz). getMinDistance() returns the
  closest object across all 64 zones in mm. IMPORTANT: when NOTHING is in range it
  returns the sentinel 32767, not -1 and not 0. So `getMinDistance() < THRESHOLD`
  already means "something is in front within THRESHOLD mm" and is false when empty.
- The most common request is "do X when something is in front" (play a sound, light
  up, show something). Implement this as a RESPONSIVE, EDGE-TRIGGERED presence detector:
    * Keep a `static bool present` across loops. Fire the action ONCE on the rising
      edge (was absent → now present). Stop/clear the action on the falling edge
      (now absent). The instant something comes back, it fires AGAIN.
    * Default trigger distance ~300mm unless the user gives a distance.
    * Use HYSTERESIS to kill boundary flicker, NOT a cooldown: enter when
      `minDist < ENTER` (e.g. 300mm), leave only when `minDist > EXIT` (e.g. 400mm).
      This debounces noise without adding any delay.
- DO NOT add a multi-second "ready again" / cooldown timer before it can re-trigger.
  Re-arm immediately on the falling edge so re-entry replays instantly. A cooldown
  makes it feel laggy and is almost never what the user wants.
- Respond within ~1 reading (~70ms). Do not gate the detection behind a slow
  EveryTimer — only rate-limit outbound stream/log events, never the trigger itself.
- Skeleton:
    static bool present = false;
    int16_t d = sensor.getMinDistance();
    if (!present && d < 300) { present = true;  /* entered: start action */ }
    else if (present && d > 400) { present = false; /* left: stop action */ }
modules.control_ui_suggestion: An 8x8 heatmap where each cell's color encodes distance (warmer = closer, cooler = farther). Above the heatmap show min/max/mean readouts in real time. Optionally overlay a hover tooltip showing exact mm per zone.

capability_detail.description: Get distance for a specific zone (0-63) in mm
Get minimum distance across all 64 zones in mm

modules.name: Rotary Encoder Knob
modules.description: Rotary encoder knob with 15 click-steps, push-button switch, and 12-LED NeoPixel indicator ring. Turn to scroll/adjust values with tactile clicks, press down to confirm. The ring automatically shows the knob position with a smooth glow/trail effect (default white, configurable). Best for menus, parameter tuning, and navigation. Use this when the user asks for a 'knob', 'dial', 'encoder', or 'scroll wheel'. Double module spanning two adjacent ports: CLK on Line A1, DT on Line B1, button (SW) on Line A2, NeoPixel ring data on Line B2.
modules.use_for: A dial you turn and press to move through menus or adjust things like volume, with a ring of lights that follows it.
modules.how_it_works:
ROTARY ENCODER KNOB:
- MUST call update() once per loop iteration — it samples the encoder, polls
  the button, AND refreshes the LED ring. Nothing updates without it.
- The encoder is decoded by the hardware pulse counter (PCNT), so no steps
  are EVER missed, even if the loop is briefly busy (display push, other
  LEDs). But the position + ring only advance when update() runs, so call it
  every loop and keep the loop moving.
- getPosition() returns cumulative int32_t. Use change detection: if (pos != lastPos).
- wasRotatedCW()/wasRotatedCCW() are edge-triggered — return true once per step.
- wasPressed() is edge-triggered for the push button. isPressed() is level-triggered.
- LED ring auto-indicates knob position. Customize with setRingColor(r, g, b).
- setRingColor/setRingBrightness/setRingPosition stage the change; it appears
  on the next update() call (so keep calling update() each loop).
- MAX 4 KNOBS: each claims one of the ESP32-S3's 4 hardware PCNT units. A 5th
  knob will not track (it logs a warning at begin()).
- LOOP RESPONSIVENESS: the ring is rendered inside update() (not a background
  task), so a SHORT loop delay — 2-5ms — keeps both the ring and any other
  outputs (grid, screen, motor) snappy. A 15-20ms delay makes the ring and
  colors visibly lag a fast spin. The encoder COUNT is never lost regardless
  (PCNT), but the visible refresh rate follows your loop.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: A circular dial gauge that rotates with incoming knob events, with the numeric value in the center. When the knob's press event fires, briefly pulse the dial ring (e.g. flash to accent color for 200ms).

modules.name: Button
modules.description: Single momentary switch on Data A, active low (pressed = LOW); Data B drives the V2.0 RGB indicator. Edge detection only — no software debounce in the driver.
modules.recommended_because: the default input; one port, full driver + measured size
modules.use_for: A button you press to start, stop or pick things.
modules.how_it_works:
BUTTON MODULE:
- You MUST call button.update() at the START of every loop iteration before checking wasPressed()/wasReleased().
  Without update(), edge detection will NEVER trigger and wasPressed() always returns false.
- wasPressed() is edge-triggered — returns true ONCE per press. Do NOT use in while() loops.
- For hold detection, use isPressed() (level-triggered) instead.
- The driver does NOT debounce in software: update() reports every level change it samples
  (button.cpp: "no software debounce - hardware capacitor handles it"), and the doc's
  "Debouncing: In driver" row is not what the shipped source does. Contact bounce slower than
  your loop is reported as extra presses — measured 2026-09-14: one
  press bouncing at 20 ms spacing produced three wasPressed() edges, so a toggle written as
  `if (wasPressed()) on = !on;` can end where it started. For any toggle/count driven by
  wasPressed(), ignore a press edge that arrives within ~40 ms of the last accepted one
  (millis() timestamp), and only redraw outputs when the state actually changed.
- Button instance names use PORT numbers (e.g., button_2 means port 2), NOT sequential indices.
  If only button_2 and button_5 exist, there is NO button_1, button_3, button_4, or button_6.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: A big round indicator that flashes the accent color for ~300ms on each press event, with a press counter beneath ('Presses: 42'). For projects with multiple buttons, render one indicator + counter per button keyed by the event key.

modules.name: I2S Speaker (MAX98357A)
modules.description: I2S audio amplifier for tones, melodies, and streamed MP3/audio playback. Double module spanning two adjacent ports: LRCLK on Line A1, BCLK on Line B1, DIN on Line B2. Uses MAX98357A 3W Class D amp. MP3/audio files are decoded on the host (browser via Web Serial, or app via WebSocket) into 16 kHz mono PCM and streamed to the device as play_pcm chunks — no on-device MP3 decoder needed.
modules.use_for: Plays beeps, tunes and other sounds.
modules.how_it_works:
SPEAKER MODULE (I2S MAX98357A):
- DEFAULT TO MELODIES, NOT BARE TONES. Almost every feedback sound (jump, click, hit,
  success, error, warning, threshold-crossed, …) should be a SHORT 2–4 NOTE SEQUENCE
  via playNote(), not a single playTone() call. A bare sustained tone is the most
  common cause of "weird static / annoying high-pitch noise" complaints.
    // Good — short success motif:
    speaker.playNote(NOTE_C5, 90);
    speaker.playNote(NOTE_E5, 90);
    speaker.playNote(NOTE_G5, 120);
    // Good — short error motif:
    speaker.playNote(NOTE_E4, 120);
    speaker.playNote(NOTE_C4, 180);
- playTone(frequency, duration_ms) plays a single sine wave for duration_ms then auto-
  stops (non-blocking). New calls reset the timer. duration_ms <= 0 means "play until
  stop()" — only use that for sustained sweeps or held notes; never as a one-shot
  feedback default.
- playNote(frequency, duration_ms) plays one note with a 15% silence gap, perfect for
  sequencing melodies. Chained calls AUTO-QUEUE (FIFO, depth 16) — back-to-back
  `playNote(C5,90); playNote(E5,90); playNote(G5,120);` plays a real melody with NO
  delay() needed between calls. Use NOTE_REST (=0) for a pause: playNote(NOTE_REST,200).
  Call speaker.stop() to interrupt and clear the queued notes.
- playChord(freqs[], n, duration_ms) plays up to 6 simultaneous frequencies for
  duration_ms then auto-stops. Use this for chords (e.g. C-E-G triad), layered notes,
  or "multiple buttons held = polyphony" patterns. Stacking playTone() calls in one
  loop iteration just overwrites the previous frequency — the user hears only the last
  one.
- playRTTTL(rtttlString) plays an RTTTL melody — non-blocking, plays in background.
  RTTTL strings look like: "name:d=4,o=5,b=140:c,e,g,2c6". Just pass the const char*.
  Prefer this for anything called a "tune", "jingle", "ringtone", "song", or "melody".
- Use NOTE_C4..NOTE_B5 (≈260–990 Hz) as the comfortable default range. Notes above
  NOTE_C6 (1047 Hz) get piercing; NEVER pass a raw freq above 2000 Hz to playTone().
  Stick to one common scale (C major or A minor) — no random Hz values.
- Use NOTE_C4, NOTE_D4, etc. constants for musical notes (defined as globals).
- setVolume(0.0–1.0) controls output level. Always call speaker.setVolume(0.4f) in
  setup() — 1.0 (the constructor default) clips on the MAX98357A and is uncomfortably
  loud. Reserve 0.8+ for explicitly user-requested "loud"/"alarm" behaviour.
- For mic-to-speaker passthrough: use speaker.writeSamples(buffer, length).
- NEVER call tone() or noTone() — those are Arduino built-ins that don't work with I2S.
- CRITICAL — DO NOT PLAY SOUNDS ON BOOT. setup() must NEVER call speaker.playTone(),
  speaker.playNote(), speaker.playChord(), or speaker.playRTTTL() (unless the user has
  explicitly requested an auto-play boot melody). At most setup() may call a single
  short blip (playTone(880, 50)) as a "ready" indicator, and only if the user asked for
  audible feedback. A device that screams a tone every time it boots is the #1 complaint
  from users — never do this by default.
- IMPORTANT: Do NOT play sounds continuously in a loop — this creates an annoying constant noise.
  Only play sounds in response to events (button press, sensor threshold, timer, incoming action).
  Use if-guards, cooldown timers, or state flags to prevent repeated triggering.
  For example: if (triggered && !alreadyPlayed) { speaker.playTone(440, 200); alreadyPlayed = true; }
- Cap individual tone durations at ≤ 2000 ms unless the user explicitly asked for a
  sustained tone. A playTone(440, 60000) call is almost always a bug — it locks the audio
  task into a one-minute sine wave that the user can't easily stop. For "play until X
  happens" patterns, use playChord (which honors live updates / stop()) and call
  speaker.stop() from the same code path that satisfies X.
- When idle, the speaker should be SILENT. Never put playTone() directly in loop() without a guard.
- MP3 / AUDIO FILE PLAYBACK: the ESP32 cannot decode MP3 itself (no decoder library is shipped).
  Instead the host (browser via Web Serial, or app via WebSocket) decodes the MP3, resamples to
  16 kHz mono int16 PCM, and streams it as a sequence of {"action":"play_pcm","value":"<base64>"}
  messages. The firmware just calls speaker.playPCMBase64(value) inside its handleMessage handler
  for the "play_pcm" action — no extra setup, no buffering on the device, no MP3 decoder. So when
  a user asks for "play a sound file / play an MP3 / stream audio", include the speaker module and
  wire up the play_pcm action; the rest is a host-side concern. Do NOT try to add ESP8266Audio,
  AudioGeneratorMP3, ESP32-audioI2S, or any on-device MP3 decoder — they break the PlatformIO build.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: A row of preset sound buttons (e.g. beep / chime / alarm) that each dispatch a play action with a sound name. Add a volume slider that sends a volume action live as it moves, and an 'Is playing' indicator driven by state events. If the project uses MP3/audio file playback (play_pcm streaming from host), add an MP3 file picker + play/stop transport in the UI.

modules.name: I2S MEMS Microphone (ICS-43434)
modules.description: I2S MEMS microphone for audio capture and sound level detection. Double module spanning two adjacent ports: LR select on Line A1, WS on Line B1, SCK on Line A2, SD on Line B2. 24-bit output, 16kHz sample rate.
modules.use_for: Listens for sound, so your project can react to claps, voices or how loud a room is.
modules.how_it_works:
MICROPHONE MODULE (I2S ICS-43434):
- getSoundLevel() returns RMS level 0-32767. Call it periodically, not in a tight loop.
- isSoundDetected(threshold) is a convenience check — default threshold is 500.
- For recording: startRecording() → wait → stopRecording() → getRecording() returns const int16_t*.
- getRecordingLength() returns sample count. Max ~10 seconds at 16kHz.
- getRecording() returns a CONST pointer — pass it to speaker.writeSamples() for playback.
- Do NOT call getRecording() without const: use "const int16_t* buf = mic.getRecording();"
- getPeakAmplitude() resets after each read — use for beat/clap detection.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: A live VU-meter bar driven by sensor-level events, plus a Record/Stop toggle that dispatches the matching action. Show a 30-second timeline of recent levels below the meter so users can see speech vs silence at a glance.

modules.name: DC Motor (H-Bridge)
modules.description: DC motor with H-bridge driver. IN1 on Line B, IN2 on Line A, as the driver is wired (the module's documentation labels them the other way round). Supports PWM speed control.
modules.use_for: Spins wheels, fans or anything else that needs to turn, at the speed you choose.
modules.how_it_works:
DC MOTOR (H-Bridge):
- forward(speed) and reverse(speed) take 0–255. stop() coasts, brake() active-stops.
- setSpeed(-255 to +255) combines direction and speed in one call.
- When motors are on OPPOSITE SIDES of a vehicle, they face opposite directions physically.
  To go straight: left motors forward(), right motors reverse() (or vice versa).
- NEVER use analogWrite() or digitalWrite() directly — always use the motor instance methods.
modules.control_ui_suggestion: A horizontal slider from -100 to +100 representing motor speed (negative = reverse) that dispatches a speed action live as it moves. Add a prominent Stop button at center-zero, and a text readout showing current direction + magnitude.

capability_detail.description: Run motor forward at specified speed (0-255)
Run motor in reverse at specified speed (0-255)
Stop the motor (coast)
Brake the motor (active stop)
Set motor speed and direction (-255 to +255)

modules.name: Stepper Motor Driver (NEMA 17 / TMC2209)
modules.description: Bipolar stepper motor (e.g. NEMA 17) driven by a TMC2209-LA-T chip in STEP/DIR mode. STEP on Line A, DIR on Line B, ENABLE on Line C. Requires an external motor power supply (typically 12-24V) wired to the driver board.
modules.use_for: Moves a motor in small, exact steps, for parts that must stop at a precise spot. Needs its own motor and power supply.
modules.how_it_works:
STEPPER MOTOR (NEMA 17 + TMC2209, STEP/DIR mode):
- All motion calls are BLOCKING — they return after the requested pulses are issued.
  Do not call them from interrupt handlers or expect concurrent updates.
- step(N, sps) moves in the current direction. Use setDirection(true|false) first,
  OR use moveSteps(signedSteps, sps) which sets direction from the sign.
- moveTo(target, sps) is relative to resetPosition() or power-on — there is no
  home switch. Always resetPosition() at a known mechanical reference if absolute
  coordinates matter.
- stepsPerSecond is clamped to [1, 20000]. Typical values: 200–2000 for smooth motion.
  Higher rates risk missed steps if the motor isn't tuned. Default is 800 sps.
- "Microsteps per revolution" depends on the TMC2209 microstep setting latched by
  MS1/MS2 on the driver board (default usually 1/8 -> 1600 microsteps/rev for a
  1.8°/step NEMA 17). When unsure, ask the user or assume 1600.
- enable() must be called before motion; the driver auto-enables on the first
  step() call. Call disable() when idle to save power and reduce heat (motor coasts).
- NEVER toggle the STEP/DIR/ENABLE pins with digitalWrite() directly — always use
  the StepperMotor instance methods.
- VMOT (motor supply) is external. Generated code cannot detect a missing supply;
  symptom is silent no-motion despite calls succeeding.

capability_detail.description: Initialise pins. Motor starts disabled (coils released).
Move N microsteps in the current direction at a given pulse rate: step(numSteps, stepsPerSecond)
Signed relative move; positive = forward, negative = reverse: moveSteps(signedSteps, stepsPerSecond)
Absolute move to a position counted from resetPosition()/power-on (no homing): moveTo(targetPosition, stepsPerSecond)
Set DIR pin without moving: setDirection(forward)
Energise coils (active-low EN -> LOW). Provides holding torque.
Release coils (active-low EN -> HIGH). Motor coasts; lower power draw.
Current signed position in microsteps: getPosition() -> int32_t
Reset the position counter to zero (no movement).

I2C modules on different ports use software I2C (bit-banging)
Port 1 uses hardware I2C (Wire) by default
Port 5 shares GPIO 43/44 with UART0 TX/RX. Prefer other ports when possible. Digital-only (no ADC).

offtheshelf_boards.name: Raspberry Pi 5
offtheshelf_boards.notes: Runs Linux, not bare-metal firmware — so the FIRMWARE phase does not apply to it. Needs a 5V/5A USB-C supply for full performance; an undersized supply throttles it in ways that read as random instability. GPIO is 3.3V and NOT 5V tolerant.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
offtheshelf_boards.notes: Linux SBC. GPIO is 3.3V and not 5V tolerant. Runs hot under sustained load — plan for a heatsink in any enclosed design.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The small, cheap Linux option. 512MB RAM is the real constraint — it is easy to specify software that will not fit.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Raspberry Pi Pico 2
offtheshelf_boards.notes: A microcontroller, NOT a Linux computer — despite the Raspberry Pi name. No wireless at all on the base model; pick the Pico 2 W if the design needs Wi-Fi. Programmable IO (PIO) blocks can bit-bang protocols the hardware peripherals do not cover.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Raspberry Pi Pico W
offtheshelf_boards.notes: RP2040 with a CYW43439 radio. GPIO25 drives the onboard LED on the non-W Pico but is wired to the radio chip here, which is a classic port-from-Pico bug.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Arduino UNO R4 WiFi
offtheshelf_boards.notes: 5V logic in the classic UNO shape, so UNO shields fit — but its 5V outputs will damage a 3v3 sensor wired directly. Level-shift, or pick a 3v3 board. Carries a 12x8 LED matrix on board.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Arduino UNO R3
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The board most people already own. 2KB of RAM and 32KB of flash is the real limit — it cannot drive a colour display or hold a TLS stack. No wireless. 5V logic; see the R4 note about 3v3 parts.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Arduino Nano ESP32
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The same silicon as the Atech motherboard in a Nano footprint, so firmware concepts port directly — but there are no ports and everything is wired by hand.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Arduino Nano
offtheshelf_boards.notes: A breadboard-friendly UNO R3 with the same ATmega328P and the same 2KB RAM ceiling.

offtheshelf_boards.name: ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The bare-board equivalent of the Atech motherboard's silicon. Same drivers compile, same toolchain — the difference is that nothing clips in.

offtheshelf_boards.name: ESP32 DevKit V1 (WROOM-32)
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The classic cheap ESP32. GPIO34-39 are INPUT ONLY, and GPIO6-11 are wired to the flash chip and must never be used — the single most common way to brick a sketch on this board.

offtheshelf_boards.name: ESP32-C3 SuperMini
offtheshelf_boards.notes: Very small and very cheap RISC-V board. Only 11 usable GPIO — count the pins the design needs before choosing it.

offtheshelf_boards.name: STM32 "Blue Pill" (F103C8T6)
offtheshelf_boards.notes: Cheap and capable, but needs an ST-Link or a flashed bootloader to program — it is not USB-plug-and-flash like an ESP32 or an Arduino. Many clones ship the wrong USB pull-up resistor.

offtheshelf_boards.name: Teensy 4.1
offtheshelf_boards.notes: The fastest board in this list by a wide margin, and the choice for audio DSP or high-rate sampling. NOT 5V tolerant despite the header size.

ky_modules.name: Photo resistor module
ky_modules.notes: LDR in a divider. Reads brighter as an INCREASING value on most KY-018 boards, but the divider orientation varies between clones — calibrate in firmware, never hardcode a threshold.

ky_modules.name: Optical broken (photo interrupter) module
ky_modules.notes: Slotted opto-interrupter. Output is a clean digital edge when something enters the slot — good for an encoder wheel or an end-stop.

ky_modules.name: Laser emitter module
ky_modules.notes: 650nm laser diode. Class 2 — never aim at an eye, and say so in safety_notes on any BOM that includes it.

ky_modules.name: Infrared emission module
ky_modules.notes: IR LED for remote-control transmit. Needs a 38kHz carrier generated in firmware (LEDC on ESP32), not a plain digitalWrite.

ky_modules.name: Infrared receiver module
ky_modules.notes: 38kHz demodulating receiver, idles HIGH and pulls LOW on carrier. Pair with KY-005 for a link, or use alone with a TV remote.

ky_modules.name: Flame sensor module
ky_modules.notes: IR photodiode tuned to ~760-1100nm. Has BOTH a digital output (threshold set by the onboard pot) and an analog one — wire D0 for a simple alarm, A0 when the design needs the level. Not a safety-certified fire detector.

ky_modules.name: Obstacle avoidance sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Reflective IR proximity, range set by two pots. Output is active LOW when an obstacle is seen. Range and reliability depend heavily on target colour — matte black absorbs the IR and reads as "clear".

ky_modules.name: Hunt (line tracking) sensor module
ky_modules.notes: TCRT5000-class reflective sensor pointed down at the floor. The classic line-follower input; use three of them for a steerable follower.

ky_modules.name: 2-color LED module (5mm)
ky_modules.notes: Two LED dies in one package sharing a common cathode — TWO GPIOs, one per colour. Driving both gives a third (orange) colour.

ky_modules.name: Yin Yi 2-color LED module (3mm)
ky_modules.notes: The 3mm sibling of KY-011. Same two-GPIO wiring.

ky_modules.name: 3-color (RGB) LED module
ky_modules.notes: Common-cathode RGB, THREE GPIOs. Needs PWM (ESP32 LEDC) on all three for colour mixing; plain digitalWrite gives only the 7 corner colours.

ky_modules.name: 3-color full-color LED SMD module
ky_modules.notes: SMD RGB, same three-GPIO wiring as KY-016. Most KY-009 boards have NO series resistors — add them or drive at reduced duty.

ky_modules.name: Automatic flashing colorful LED module
ky_modules.notes: Self-flashing LED: the colour cycle is inside the die, so firmware can only turn it on and off. Cannot be used to show a specific colour.

ky_modules.name: Magic light cup module
ky_modules.notes: Sold as a PAIR. Each board has an LED plus a mercury tilt switch, so it is both an input and an output — the "magic" is firmware fading one cup's LED as the other tilts.

ky_modules.name: Small passive buzzer module
ky_modules.notes: PASSIVE — it has no oscillator, so it makes no sound on a steady HIGH and needs a square wave at the target frequency (ESP32 LEDC tone). This is the one to pick for melodies. Confusing it with KY-012 is the classic failure.

ky_modules.name: Active buzzer module
ky_modules.notes: ACTIVE — the oscillator is built in, so a plain HIGH makes its one fixed tone. Cannot play a melody. Pick this for a beep, KY-006 for music.

ky_modules.name: Microphone sound sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Electret mic with an LM393 comparator. D0 is a clap/threshold trigger set by the pot; A0 is an envelope, NOT audio — it cannot record or recognise speech, only loudness.

ky_modules.name: Sensitive microphone sensor module
ky_modules.notes: The high-sensitivity sibling of KY-038, larger mic element. Same two outputs, same limitation: loudness only, not audio capture.

ky_modules.name: Vibration switch module
ky_modules.notes: Spring switch that closes momentarily on a knock. The pulse is very short — poll fast or use an interrupt, or the event is missed.

ky_modules.name: Hit (knock) sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Spring-contact knock sensor, same class as KY-002 and the same short-pulse trap.

ky_modules.name: Tilt switch module
ky_modules.notes: Ball-rolling tilt switch. Gives orientation past a threshold angle only — it cannot report an ANGLE. Use an IMU for that.

ky_modules.name: Mercury open optical module
ky_modules.notes: Mercury tilt switch. Contains liquid mercury — restricted under RoHS in the EU and must not be shipped in a product. Prefer KY-020 (ball type) for anything the user will actually build; flag it in safety_notes if used.

ky_modules.name: Detect the heartbeat module
ky_modules.notes: IR finger-transmission pulse sensor. Very noisy — needs filtering and a steady finger. NOT a medical device; never present its output as a clinical measurement.

ky_modules.name: XY-axis joystick module
ky_modules.notes: TWO analog axes plus a push-button — so it needs TWO ADC1 pins and one digital pin, three GPIOs total. The most pin-hungry part in the kit.

ky_modules.name: Rotary encoder module
ky_modules.notes: Quadrature encoder plus a push-button: THREE GPIOs (CLK, DT, SW). Needs debouncing or interrupt handling; a naive poll loses counts when turned quickly.

ky_modules.name: Key switch (button) module
ky_modules.notes: Momentary tactile button with an onboard pull-up. Debounce in firmware.

ky_modules.name: Metal touch sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Transistor-amplified metal touch pad. Independent of the ESP32's own capacitive touch peripheral — it is a plain digital input here.

ky_modules.name: Hall magnetic sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Digital Hall switch — magnet present or not. POLARITY-SENSITIVE: it responds to one pole only, so a magnet that "does not work" is usually just the wrong way round.

ky_modules.name: Linear magnetic Hall sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Linear Hall: A0 varies with field STRENGTH and polarity around a mid-scale idle, which makes it usable as a proximity or current sensor. D0 is the thresholded version.

ky_modules.name: Class Bihor magnetic sensor module
ky_modules.notes: Analog Hall (AH49E-class), bipolar around a mid-scale rest value.

ky_modules.name: Mini magnetic reed module
ky_modules.notes: Reed switch — a mechanical contact closed by a nearby magnet. Unlike the Hall parts it is not polarity-sensitive. The standard door/window sensor.

ky_modules.name: Reed module
ky_modules.notes: Full-size reed switch with both digital and analog outputs. Same job as KY-021 in a larger package.

ky_modules.name: Analog temperature sensor module (thermistor)
ky_modules.notes: NTC thermistor in a divider. Converting the reading to °C needs the Steinhart-Hart equation and the part's B-value — an ADC count is not a temperature.

ky_modules.name: Temperature sensor module (DS18B20)
ky_modules.notes: DS18B20 on a 1-Wire bus — a true digital °C reading, no calibration maths, and several can share ONE GPIO by address. The best temperature part in the kit. Needs a 4.7k pull-up (present on most KY-001 boards).

ky_modules.name: Temperature sensor module (thermistor + comparator)
ky_modules.notes: NTC thermistor with an LM393 threshold output. D0 is a "too hot" trigger set by the pot; A0 needs the same Steinhart-Hart conversion as KY-013.

ky_modules.name: Temperature and humidity sensor module (DHT11)
ky_modules.notes: DHT11 on a single-wire proprietary protocol — needs a DHT library, not a plain read. Slow (one sample per ~2s) and coarse (±2°C, ±5% RH). The Atech aht20_sensor is far more accurate if that tier is available.

ky_modules.name: 5V relay module
ky_modules.notes: 5V single-channel relay with a flyback diode and driver transistor on board. The coil needs 5V (not 3v3) and ~70mA, so it is powered from the 5V rail while its signal pin is driven from a 3v3 GPIO. If it switches MAINS voltage, that is a hazard which MUST appear in safety_notes.

ky_source.kit: 37 in 1 Sensors Modules Arduino Starter Kit
ky_source.note: Sold as one kit, not per module. A BOM line for any single KY module is fulfilled by buying this kit, so `est_price_eur` on a KY line is the kit price where the user owns none of it — never a per-module invention.
